newsitem.title: UK: Democrat gains seen depressing dollar and bonds.
newsitem.headline: Democrat gains seen depressing dollar and bonds.

text.p: If President Bill Clinton's Democrats make gains in the race to control the U.S. Congress, the dollar and Treasuries are expected to ease slightly in the short term, a Reuters survey of economists showed on Tuesday.
The poll showed that a Democratic victory in either the Senate or the House of Representatives would have more of a negative effect than if Republicans retained control of both.
Out of 27 experts polled, 24 predicted that the dollar would ease against the mark and 23 said they expected an easing against the yen if the Democrats made Congressional gains.
Taking an average of the predictions, the falls would be slightly less than a pfennig against the mark and less than one yen on Monday's trading levels, according to the survey.
All but one of 26 of those questioned about Treasuries said they expected the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond to rise.
The average of the forecasts was 6.73 percent, nine basis points higher than Tuesday's market.

The survey predicted the effects of Democratic gains would be minimal and would rapidly be discounted as Clinton -- seen as the almost certain victor in the presidential election -- prepares for his second term at the White House. "The status quo would be a good result for the markets...Bonds would probably come off a point or two on the Democrats taking the House," said David Brown, chief European economist for Bear Stearns International in London.
The economists predicted on average that the dollar would trade at 1.5043 marks and 112.98 yen if the Democrats gained control of at least one of the chambers on Capitol Hill.
At 1530 GMT on Tuesday the U.S. currency was trading at 1.5150 marks and 113.88 yen.
As Americans began voting on Tuesday, Clinton was relatively confident of winning a second term and Republican challenger Bob Dole was hoping for an upset victory.

Political pundits and economists, nearly unanimous in anticipating a Clinton vitory, were watching the Congressional race closely to see if the incumbent could expect to find a political friend or foe at the other end of Pennsylvania Avenue.
Late polls said the Republicans seemed likely to retain control of the 100-member Senate, but the 435-seat House of Representatives was rated too close to call.

"It would be hard to envisage a clean sweep. The Democrats are currently already finding the going harder in their attempts to retake Congress," said Tim Fox, Treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.
Many of the economists surveyed pointed out that the effects of Democratic gains in Congress would swiftly be discounted.

"In the very short-term, there will be a sell-off on the dollar (if the Democratic Party made gains in Congress). But it will be very marginal," said James Stewart, chief economist at S-E-Banken in London.
"Once the markets have digested the information, the conclusion will be that on the fiscal side, there will be a little bit more laxity," he said.

"I'm not sure if it will make a huge difference whoever wins Congress. It will have no effect on monetary policy, although perhaps on fiscal policy," said Nigel Richardson, economist at Yamaichi Bank in London.
"My gut feeling is that if we are to see a negative reaction it will be on Treasuries. But we are not going to see a major bear market developing -- maybe a couple of points at the maximum," he said.
